hops.title: Say it: a carrot is an underground lunchbox
hops.text: Try saying, "A carrot is the plant's underground lunchbox, packed with sugar so it can grow flowers and seeds next spring." Use it when you hold up a carrot together. A carrot plant usually makes seeds in its second growing season. In its first season it fills its root with sugar, and that is when farmers pull it up.

sources.citation: Washington State University, Ask Dr. Universe, "Why do carrots have sugar?" (2025)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Freshly pulled orange carrots with feathery green tops beside a small open lunchbox on a sunny wooden step.
image.caption: A carrot packs sugar into its root in its first season to grow flowers and seeds in its second.

hops.title: Compare it: a stem and a bundle of drinking straws
hops.text: Hold a fistful of drinking straws upright with your child. A stem is packed with tiny tubes that carry water from the soil up to the leaves, a lot like those straws standing together. They do big work: a big oak tree can move about 40,000 gallons of water up through its trunk and out its leaves in a year.

sources.citation: U.S. Geological Survey, Water Science School, "Evapotranspiration and the Water Cycle"
Texas A&M Forest Service, "Trees of Texas: How Trees Grow"

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A parent and child seen from behind beneath a tall oak tree, the parent holding a bundle of drinking straws upright.
image.caption: Tiny tubes in stems carry water; a big oak can move 40,000 gallons a year.

hops.title: Ask it: what would your rule for a fruit be?
hops.text: When you spot a tomato, ask, "If you made the rule for what counts as a fruit, what would it be?" Some kids say sweet, the way cooks often sort food. Tell them it is good thinking. Grown-ups argue too: in 1893 the U.S. Supreme Court called tomatoes vegetables for an import tax, while noting botanists call them fruit.

sources.citation: U.S. Supreme Court, Nix v. Hedden, 149 U.S. 304 (1893), via Cornell Law School Legal Information Institute

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A bright red tomato and a green cucumber on a wooden kitchen table beside a wooden judge's gavel.
image.caption: In 1893 the Supreme Court called tomatoes vegetables for a tax, while noting botanists call them fruit.
